The thousand words begin with the hum of a library after closing. The lights are still on, but the chairs have been pushed in, and the air holds the smell of paper, dust, and rain drying on coat sleeves. I am supposed to write whatever comes to me, which is a strange instruction, because what comes first is not a thought but a feeling: the sensation of standing in a room where everyone has just left. There is a residue to silence like that. It is not empty. It is full of small evidence—a pencil on the table, a receipt used as a bookmark, a page turned down at the corner. I think about the person who left each object and wonder whether they meant to return. Most of us mean to return. Most of us do not.

Outside, the street is shining. Rain has made the asphalt into a dark mirror, and the traffic lights bleed green and red across it. A bus sighs at the corner, opens its doors, closes them, and moves on with almost no one inside. I like the city best at this hour, when it has stopped performing and has become merely itself. The bakery is shutting its shutters. The flower shop has brought its buckets inside. A man in a yellow raincoat walks a small dog that refuses to hurry. None of this is important, and that is exactly why I want to save it. The significant moments are always being photographed, but the ordinary ones are the ones that make a life feel lived.

I have been given a thousand words, and I keep thinking of all the things that cannot fit into them. A thousand words cannot hold my mother’s hands, which are smaller now than I remember and always cold in winter. It cannot hold the sound of a friend laughing on the other end of a bad telephone line, or the exact color of the sky above a parking lot in Ohio when I was nineteen and certain my life was about to begin. Words are generous and stingy at once. They let us say almost anything, but they leave a gap between what we mean and what lands on the page. We spend our lives trying to close that gap, and sometimes, for a sentence or two, we almost do.

What comes to me next is a memory of a train. I was traveling from one city to another, and a woman across the aisle was reading a book with a green cover. She read with her finger moving under the lines, as if she were keeping time. Every few pages she would stop, look out the window, and then go back to reading. I never learned her name. I never spoke to her. But I remember her more clearly than some people I have known for years. This happens, I think, because certain strangers carry a version of us we recognize. She looked the way I feel when I am reading something true: absent from the room and more present than ever.

The rain starts again, tapping the library windows with a sound like fingernails on a table. I open a book at random. It is a history of maps, and the first sentence says that every map is a lie that tells the truth. I close it again. That is how I feel about writing. We arrange events into beginnings and endings because it comforts us, even though life keeps refusing to stay in order. We leave out the hours spent waiting, the arguments about groceries, the days when nothing happens and the nothing is so heavy we mistake it for sadness. But maybe those are the real maps: the small decisions, the unremarkable afternoons, the way we choose one street over another and meet someone who changes everything.

I start to make a list of things I would put in a time capsule for no one in particular. The smell of a new box of crayons. The sound of a screen door slamming. A train ticket with the edge torn. The phrase “I’ll be right back.” A recipe card in someone else’s handwriting. The first cold day of autumn, when you wear a sweater and immediately regret it by noon. A song that reminds you of a summer you did not appreciate enough. A library book returned late. A glass of water brought to you when you did not ask. The list grows until it becomes a kind of prayer, though I am not sure to whom. Maybe gratitude is just attention paid twice.

The librarian returns from the back office and looks at the clock. It is almost time. She does not tell me to leave, but she begins turning off the lights in sections, and the room goes darker in stages, like a sentence being revised. I gather my things. On my way out, I pass the display table where the staff have arranged books about weather. I pick one up and put it back. I have enough to carry already. In the doorway, the cool air hits my face. The street is still shining. The man with the dog is gone. The bakery is dark. I stand under the awning for a moment, not wanting to step into the rain and not wanting to stay.

This is where the thousand words end, though nothing really ends here. Tomorrow the library will open again. Someone will turn down a page. Someone will forget a receipt. Someone will read a sentence that changes the shape of their day. I will probably write about something else. But for now, the rain, the bus, the yellow raincoat, the green-covered book—all of it stays with me, a small city inside a single paragraph. If you asked me what I meant by any of this, I would say I meant only to pay attention, and to leave a light on for whatever comes next.

If you asked me what I meant by any of this, I would say I meant only to pay attention, and to leave a light on for whatever comes next.
